Land Use Permits and Appeals in Washington: Why the Deadline Decides Most Cases

7 min read·Justin D. Leigh, Attorney-at-Law

A notice appears on a pole at the edge of the lot behind your house, describing something you have to read three times to understand. Or you are on the other side of it, a year and real money into a project at a county planning department, and a neighbor has just filed something. The first question a lawyer asks is not whether the decision was right. It is what date it issued, because a Washington land use permit appeal runs on a clock measured in days, and once that clock expires the merits stop mattering.

Who actually writes the rules that govern your property

Washington land use regulation is local, with a statutory frame around it. Under the Growth Management Act, chapter 36.70A RCW, planning counties and cities adopt a comprehensive plan with mandatory elements that include land use, housing, capital facilities, utilities, and transportation, and they must then act in conformity with that plan. RCW 36.70A.070; RCW 36.70A.120.

The plan is policy about how areas are intended to develop over twenty years, while the zoning code and the development regulations are the enforceable rules a planner applies to an application, so a parcel whose plan designation contemplates multifamily housing is not thereby zoned for it. That distinction also decides the forum. A challenge to a plan or a development regulation itself goes to the Growth Management Hearings Board within sixty days after publication, RCW 36.70A.290(2), while a challenge to a particular permit decision goes to superior court.

How a project permit gets processed

Chapter 36.70B RCW governs local project review. Within twenty-eight calendar days of receiving an application, the local government must tell the applicant in writing whether it is procedurally complete, and the statute says expressly that this determination is not a substantive review and is not conditioned on the adequacy, accuracy, or sufficiency of what was submitted. RCW 36.70B.070(1), (2). A notice of application follows within fourteen days, stating a comment period of not less than fourteen and not more than thirty days, and a project needing permits in more than one category gets a single open record hearing and no more than one closed record appeal. RCW 36.70B.110(2); RCW 36.70B.120(2). That is the whole window in which an ordinary member of the public participates, and it closes before most people have formed a view about the project.

Who decides a conditional use, a variance, or a rezone?

It depends on the local code, and the statute explaining why is worth knowing. A code city may adopt a hearing examiner system and vest in the examiner authority over conditional uses, variances, subdivisions, shoreline permits, administrative appeals, and SEPA appeals, and counties have parallel authority. RCW 35A.63.170(1); RCW 36.70.970.

Here is the part that catches people. The city's ordinance must specify the legal effect of the examiner's decisions, and the statute offers three choices: a recommendation to the legislative body, an administrative decision appealable to the legislative body, or, except for a rezone, the final decision of the legislative body. RCW 35A.63.170(2). The same kind of application can be a recommendation in one city and a final decision in the next one over, so whether a further local appeal exists is answered by reading that jurisdiction's code. Rezones add a wrinkle, because a site-specific rezone is quasi-judicial while area-wide rezones and annexations are legislative approvals the judicial review statute excludes from the definition of a land use decision. RCW 36.70C.020(2)(a).

SEPA review and what a threshold determination really is

The State Environmental Policy Act, chapter 43.21C RCW, overlays all of this. A threshold determination is required for any proposal that meets the definition of an action and is not categorically exempt, the lead agency's responsible official makes it, and it is documented as either a determination of nonsignificance or a determination of significance. WAC 197-11-310(1), (2), (5). It is due no later than ninety days after the application is complete. RCW 43.21C.033(1).

The substance is narrower than people assume. The responsible official reviews the environmental checklist, decides whether the proposal is likely to have a probable significant adverse environmental impact, and considers mitigation the agency or the applicant will implement as part of the proposal. WAC 197-11-330(1). A determination of nonsignificance is therefore not a finding that a project has no environmental effects. It is a determination that the effects, with mitigation folded in, do not rise to probable significant adverse impacts. Neighbors read a DNS as a whitewash and applicants read it as a clearance, and both overstate it.

The appeal deadline: the Land Use Petition Act

A Washington land use permit appeal that reaches court does so under chapter 36.70C RCW, which may be cited as the land use petition act and is the exclusive means of judicial review of land use decisions, subject to listed exceptions. RCW 36.70C.005; RCW 36.70C.030(1). Three features of it decide most cases before anyone argues about zoning.

What counts as the decision. A land use decision is a final determination by the local jurisdiction's body or officer with the highest level of authority to make it, including those with authority to hear appeals. RCW 36.70C.020(2). If the local code provides an appeal to a hearing examiner, the planner's letter is generally not the land use decision and the examiner's ruling generally is. Where a timely motion for reconsideration is filed, the land use decision occurs when the decision on reconsideration is entered.

The clock, and that it governs service too. A land use petition "is barred, and the court may not grant review," unless it is both timely filed with the court and timely served on the parties the statute lists, which include the local jurisdiction, each applicant and property owner named in the written decision, and each person named in the decision who appealed to a local quasi-judicial decision maker. RCW 36.70C.040(2). The petition is timely if filed and served on all of them within twenty-one days of the issuance of the land use decision. RCW 36.70C.040(3). Issuance has its own definition, three days after a written decision is mailed, or if it is not mailed, the date the jurisdiction gives notice that the decision is publicly available. RCW 36.70C.040(4)(a).

That structure is what hurts people. The deadline is short, it is unforgiving, it requires completed service rather than merely filing, and it runs from a statutory issuance date instead of the day you found out. I am giving the figure from the current statutory text, and you should still confirm both the deadline and its starting point against the statute as it reads today and against the specific local code, because the code determines which decision in the chain is final, and that determines when the clock started.

What the court can do. Review is not a second hearing. The superior court sits without a jury, reviews the record, and may grant relief only if the petitioner establishes one of six standards, running from unlawful procedure and erroneous interpretation of law to a lack of substantial evidence. RCW 36.70C.130(1). Standing is limited, and a person who is not the applicant or owner must show that the decision prejudices them, that their interests were among those the jurisdiction had to consider, and that they have exhausted their administrative remedies to the extent required by law. RCW 36.70C.060(2).

Where this goes wrong

The neighbor who learns about the project too late. Participation happens during the comment period in the notice of application, under notice methods that include posting the property, newspaper publication, and mailing to neighboring owners. RCW 36.70B.110(2), (4). Someone who misses all of it faces two problems rather than one, because the twenty-one-day clock may already be running and the exhaustion requirement may bar them even inside it. RCW 36.70C.060(2)(d).

The applicant who builds during an appeal. A stay is available but never automatic, and a court may grant one only on findings that the requesting party is likely to prevail, will suffer irreparable harm without it, that a stay will not substantially harm other parties, and that the request is timely. RCW 36.70C.100(2). Without a stay, construction proceeds at the owner's risk.

Failure to exhaust. Where the local code provides an administrative appeal, it is a prerequisite rather than an option, and skipping it ends the case without a ruling on anything.

Vesting assumptions that do not hold. A valid and fully complete building permit application is considered under the ordinances in effect on the date of application, and the same holds for preliminary plats and short plats. RCW 19.27.095(1); RCW 58.17.033(1). Two qualifications undercut the confident version of that rule. What counts as fully complete is defined by local ordinance, which is not the same thing as procedural completeness under RCW 36.70B.070, and vesting does not restrict conditions imposed under SEPA. RCW 19.27.095(2), (6); RCW 58.17.033(3).

Why this is lawyer work

Most of the work in a Washington land use permit appeal happens before any argument about the merits. Someone has to read the local code to identify which decision is the final land use decision, assemble and serve the correct party list under RCW 36.70C.040(2), decide whether the real target is the project decision, the regulation, or a SEPA determination, and get the administrative record before the court. Getting any one of those wrong forecloses the rest. On the applicant side the job runs in reverse, building a record during the local process that can survive review.

About my practice

If a decision just issued

If you have received a land use decision, or just learned that one issued, the date on it is the first thing to look at, and a Washington land use permit appeal is not something to start late. My office offers a free initial consultation by appointment in downtown Spokane.
